problem: The trap flags a correct expression. With column vectors, M = R · T means T (the translation) is applied first, so writing R · T when the translation happens first is exactly right, not a mistake. A student following this trap will build the wrong matrix.
fix: Writing M = T · R when the translation happens first. The factor nearest the point, on the right, acts first, so the translation matrix must sit on the right: M = R · T.

problem: The heading announces rotation and translation, but the worked matrices show rotation R(90°) combined with scaling S. Translation appears only in the closing sentence, so the heading does not match the example the student actually checks.
fix: Either retitle the section 'Order matters: rotation and scaling do not commute' and mention translation separately, or keep the heading and add the 3×3 version T(2, 0) · R(90°) against R(90°) · T(2, 0) as the main example.

problem: The count switches from 'matrix-vector products' to 'multiplies'. One matrix-vector product is nine multiplications, so '10,000 multiplies instead of 30,000' misstates the unit of the comparison.
fix: With k = 3 and n = 10,000 that is about 10,000 matrix-vector products instead of 30,000, plus two cheap 3×3 matrix products to build M once.

problem: The blocks run left to right as T(−px, −py) → R(θ) → T(px, py) → M, that is, in application order. The chapter's rule says the product is written with the last-applied matrix on the left, so a student can read the picture as M = T(−px, −py) · R(θ) · T(px, py), which is the wrong matrix.
fix: Reverse the block order so the product reads as written — T(px, py), then R(θ), then T(−px, −py), then M — or keep the drawing and label it 'applied in this order; in the product the rightmost factor acts first'.
